original_question: Extend the symplectomorphism and Kahler-map properties of the Madelung transform to wave functions that are allowed to vanish, and explain the quantization-condition controversy in momentum-map terms for the relevant semidirect product action.
target_in_paper: Section 14, Problem 37: extend the Madelung-transform symplectomorphism/Kähler-map results from nonvanishing wave functions to wave functions with zeros, and explain the quantization-condition controversy in momentum-map language for the same semidirect product action.
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s exact target. It correctly identifies the two-part open problem in Section 14: (i) extending the symplectomorphism/Kähler-map results for the Madelung transform to wave functions that vanish somewhere on M, and (ii) interpreting the quantization-condition controversy via the momentum-map picture for the relevant semidirect product action. It also stays in the scalar Madelung setting and does not drift into broader neighboring problems.
missing_details: The paper states the problem on an n-dimensional manifold M and uses the spaces PC∞(M, C) and Dens(M); your draft should name these spaces explicitly so the question is stand-alone.
The known symplectic result being extended is specifically the symplectomorphism between PC∞(M, C\{0}) and T*Dens(M), not an unspecified symplectic correspondence.

The Kähler statement should specify the geometric structures involved: the canonical symplectic structure and Sasaki-Fisher-Rao metric on T*Dens(M), and the natural symplectic structure and Fubini-Study metric on PC∞(M, C\{0}).
The projective nature of the wave-function space matters: PC∞(M, C) consists of cosets [ψ] of the unit L2-sphere, so the phase is only relevant up to global constant phase.
The momentum-map part should explicitly mention that wave functions are regarded as half-densities and that the group is the semidirect product of diffeomorphisms and smooth functions.

The draft does not say that the problem is to extend the already-known nonvanishing theory as narrowly stated in the paper, rather than to develop a broader theory for arbitrary singularities or for multicomponent/spinor Madelung transforms.

To be fully stand-alone, the question should make clear that the obstruction created by zeros is precisely the new issue, since the paper’s preceding paragraph states the existing results only for nonvanishing wave functions.

There are no algebraic degree, homogeneity, field, or nilpotency hypotheses in this problem; the omitted data are geometric: manifold, smoothness class, projectivization, metrics, symplectic structures, and group action.
refined_question: Let M be an n-dimensional manifold, let PC∞(M, C) denote the projective space of smooth complex-valued wave functions on M, whose elements are cosets [ψ] of the unit L2-sphere, and let Dens(M) be the space of smooth probability densities. For nonvanishing wave functions, the Madelung transform is known to induce a symplectomorphism between PC∞(M, C\{0}) and T*Dens(M), and in fact a Kähler map when T*Dens(M) is equipped with its canonical symplectic structure and Sasaki-Fisher-Rao metric while PC∞(M, C\{0}) carries its natural symplectic structure and the Fubini-Study metric. Can one extend these symplectomorphism and Kähler-map results to wave functions ψ that are allowed to have zeros on M, and at the same time explain the quantization-condition controversy in the language of the momentum map for the semidirect product action of diffeomorphisms and smooth functions on wave functions viewed as half-densities?
justification: This is the exact open problem stated in the paper. The draft tracks Problem 37 almost verbatim, but it omits the precise spaces and structures supplied by the immediately preceding paragraph in Section 14: the definition of PC∞(M, C), the role of T*Dens(M), the nonvanishing restriction PC∞(M, C\{0}), the canonical symplectic/Fubini-Study/Sasaki-Fisher-Rao structures, and the momentum-map interpretation for the semidirect product of diffeomorphisms and smooth functions acting on wave functions as half-densities. Adding those details makes the question self-contained while keeping it exactly as narrow as the paper’s intent. The paper does not formulate an explicitly equivalent alternate version of Problem 37, so no alternate formulation should be introduced.
